Alors que la riposte peine encore à freiner la progression du virus Bundibugyo, l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) et les autorités congolaises accélèrent le lancement d’essais cliniques de traitements et de vaccins.

items.title: The Catholic Church’s New Schism
items.description: At an open-air Mass in Écône, Switzerland, before a crowd of about 16,000 people, four priests became bishops last month. The men professed their fidelity to tradition against “heretics, schismatics, and those who rebel against our Holy Father.” They did so knowing full well that, in becoming bishops, they lacked something the Catholic Church deems essential: permission from the pope. All four of these men are members of the Society of Saint Pius X, or SSPX, an arch-traditionalist group of clergy founded in 1970 by the French archbishop Marcel Lefebvre. For decades, SSPX has battled with the Vatican over the group’s fear that, as one theologian told me, “in reading the signs of the times, the Catholic Church is more beholden to the times than she is a light to the nations.” Now tensions have reached a breaking point. The Vatican warned SSPX before the Écône Mass that consecrating bishops without a papal mandate would be considered a “schismatic act,” a formal separation from the Catholic Church. After the Mass, the Church issued a decree saying that the new bishops, plus the two who ordained them, incurred an automatic excommunication: They can neither receive communion nor celebrate licit Masses nor officiate valid marriages and confessions. The 700 or so SSPX priests worldwide will also fall into schism, and thereby be excommunicated, if they remain with the society. Even lay churchgoers who “formally adhere” to the group may face the same sanction. [ Read: The real religious ‘renewal’ happening in Gen Z ] By some estimates , 25,000 people in the United States are affiliated with SSPX—a tiny fraction of the roughly 53 million American Catholic adults. Many Catholics may not even know that the Church finds itself in arguably its largest schism since the 19th century. Nonetheless, the SSPX excommunications touch on broader disputes in Catholicism today: about reform, orthodoxy, and whether the Church’s institutional changes of the past half century have been for the better. That is, this schism is about more than just SSPX. It’s also about how the Church will respond to a larger group of traditionalists—those who, though still Catholic, have questioned or even attacked many of the beliefs and practices that characterize the faith today. SSPX’s fight with the Catholic Church began as a response to the Second Vatican Council, or Vatican II, the most pivotal event of 20th-century Catholic history. From 1962 to 1965, the Church instituted a series of reforms that reimagined its role in a secular age. Perhaps most famous was the council’s overhaul of the Mass in hopes of increasing participation among the faithful . In most Masses, priests stopped facing the altar and began facing the people. The local language replaced Latin as the main tongue of worship. In some parishes, out went Gregorian chants and in came guitars. Vatican II also reformed the doctrine of extra ecclesiam nulla salus , or “outside the Church, there is no salvation.” As Larry Chapp, a former theology professor at DeSales University, told me, the council clarified that Catholics “have to be open to the movement of grace outside of the boundaries of the Church.” Guided by this vision, Vatican II produced writings that promoted religious freedom , ecumenical efforts with other Christians, and “dialogue and collaboration” with non-Christian religions. To SSPX, these changes were calamitous. The society’s 28-page profession of faith asserts that true Catholicism rejects ecumenical and interfaith dialogue, and states that other faiths are “false religions” and “the work of the devil.” SSPX also holds fast to the pre–Vatican II Traditional Latin Mass as the only legitimate liturgy: The profession of faith declares that the vernacular Mass “favours heresy, weakens the faith,” and “turns the faithful away from the adoration due to God.” Lefebvre participated in Vatican II himself—he even signed all of the writings that SSPX now objects to. But he soon started denouncing the council’s reforms. Five years after the council concluded, he founded SSPX with the mission of training priests in preconciliar beliefs and practices. In 1974, Lefebvre condemned Vatican II for contributing to “the destruction of the Church,” one of the many accusations and acts of defiance that prompted Church authorities to revoke his permission to run the society. Lefebvre kept recruiting priests anyway. By 1988, SSPX had approximately 200 clergy worldwide, mainly in France, Switzerland, and the United States. In June of that year, Lefebvre ordained four priests as bishops, ignoring Pope John Paul II’s orders not to. The pontiff excommunicated Lefebvre and the four bishops but declared no formal schism. Lefebvre, for his part, continued leading the society—and vehemently opposing Vatican II, which he described as the “adulterous marriage of the Church with liberal ideas”—until his death in 1991. [ Read: The first Millennial saint ] The Vatican let SSPX exist in a kind of limbo state in the years after the 1988 excommunications. Members of the society were officially limited in the sacraments that they could officiate, but SSPX kept ordaining priests and holding illicit Masses. And yet they were still, technically, a part of the Catholic Church. Church leaders, Chapp said, made “efforts to bring them back into the fold.” In 2009, Pope Benedict XVI lifted the excommunications of the four living SSPX bishops that John Paul II had effected two decades prior. A few years later, Pope Francis granted SSPX priests permission to hear confessions and officiate marriages. Still, SSPX has no interest in being part of a Church that doesn’t spurn Vatican II. The society holds that the council’s reforms create a “state of necessity” that allows it to do what it must “to preserve the faith.” This is the irony at the heart of SSPX’s theology: The society claims to be a bulwark of the Catholic faith; it also dismisses the pope’s authority as the final interpreter of that faith. “This is not a trivial issue,” Chapp said. “Staying in union with the vicar of Christ is a central defining feature of what it means to be Catholic.” Although SSPX considers itself a lone defender of tradition, other prominent Catholics—including popes—have expressed concerns about the liturgy and emphasized the importance of doctrinal clarity. Before his pontificate, Pope Benedict XVI worried that Vatican II’s liturgical changes, as implemented, had in some situations downplayed the “authentic inner vibrancy” of the Mass. John Paul II was a consistent proponent of interfaith dialogue, but nonetheless cautioned in 1990 against “a religious relativism which leads to the belief that ‘one religion is as good as another.’” But these popes—and many other Catholics who have raised questions about the implementation of certain Church reforms—were working within the Church, not against it. SSPX, by contrast, “doesn’t have to wrestle with unclarity or ambiguity,” Father Gregory Pine, a professor of moral theology at the Dominican House of Studies in Washington, D.C., told me. It doesn’t do the hard theological work of interpreting new teachings alongside tradition. It simply maintains a posture of rejection—and calls it orthodoxy. It’s one thing for a tiny sect to go rogue. But traditionalism has many supporters in the broader Catholic Church—which means that how the Church moves forward has implications not only for SSPX but also for this larger set of traditionalists, and for the unity of the Church as a whole. Like SSPX, some traditionalists have been viciously critical of the pope, especially during Francis’s pontificate. On a 2024 visit to Singapore, for example, the late pontiff met with an interfaith group of youth and said that “all religions are paths to God”—an off-the-cuff comment that reflected a Vatican II teaching that non-Christian religions “often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all.” Still, several prominent Catholic traditionalists denounced Francis. One said that he spouted “heresy that flies in the face of Jesus Christ.” Another created a video titled “Pope Francis Is a Heretic Denying Tradition, Part 2” that echoed arguments SSPX had made before. The Traditional Latin Mass also has a following beyond SSPX. Roughly 1 million American Catholic adults attend it weekly, which is just 2 percent of the country’s overall Catholic adult population but still many more people than are affiliated with the society. The SSPX excommunications contain a clear message to all traditionalists: Vatican II itself is not up for debate. The council’s teachings and reforms are essential components of the faith, not optional addenda to it. Some Catholics believe that the Church should also continue its official position of limiting access to the Traditional Latin Mass. The Catholic writer Mike Lewis told me that support for the liturgy tends to come with an “entire theological structure” that questions the authority of Vatican II and, by extension, the pope. [ Read: What the fastest-growing Christian group says about America ] Father Pine, however, said that some proponents of the Traditional Latin Mass are simply looking for a liturgy that is “celebrated worthily” and at a “transcendent register.” And some Church leaders have signaled an openness to the Traditional Latin Mass in the weeks since the excommunications. Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone—whom Pope Leo XIV recently appointed to the Vatican’s highest court—has called for “more access” to the liturgy, and some U.S. bishops have promoted it as part of their pleas to SSPX’s followers to return to the Church. Leo XIV has stressed unity since he became pope, last year, and he has not made his position on the Traditional Latin Mass fully known. In excommunicating SSPX, he rebuked a small group of the most vocal supporters of the Traditional Latin Mass. But he has also met with a well-known proponent of the liturgy, as well as with the authors of a forthcoming book that argues that Traditional Latin Mass–goers aren’t the recalcitrants their critics make them out to be. Excommunication, the theologians I spoke with told me, serves a dual purpose: It’s punitive, but it’s also medicinal, meant to call a person or group back to communion. SSPX’s lay members, by early indications , plan to remain in schism for the time being. Those who return, though, may well find their Church to be a bit more open to traditionalism than they imagined it would be.

items.title: One Problem With Attacking the Smithsonian? Americans Like It.
items.description: Earlier this year, I visited a “ Freedom Truck ,” one of the patriotic mobile museums that the Trump administration is sending around the country for the nation’s 250 birthday. There, I had a wide-ranging conversation with a visitor who complained that the U.S. education system is not teaching what she called true history. But when I mentioned the Smithsonian, her disposition changed entirely. She’d heard rumors about “a lot of liberalism going through the Smithsonian now,” she told me, but added, “I love the Smithsonian. I don’t have a problem with it.” I hear this a lot, actually. Even now, as the museum complex continues to face a pressure campaign from the White House, public fondness for the Smithsonian—for its free entry and eclectic collections—is hard to break among those otherwise receptive to President Trump’s anti-institutionalism. Attacks on the credibility of institutions, especially those that disseminate information—universities, public schools, media organizations—have become commonplace in this so-called post-truth age. Recent data from Gallup , published last month, suggested that confidence in the majority of institutions asked about in the survey, including newspapers, public schools, and TV news, is at or near historic lows. Pollsters, meanwhile, don’t even include museums in the Gallup surveys. Although museums have certainly faced some criticism from the left and right, until now, they’ve been largely immune to the most deleterious effects of the culture wars. This may be because most Americans, unlike the president, seem to trust these entities to do their thing. A YouGov survey last week found that 57 percent of Americans said that the amount of influence the president should have over exhibits and programming at federally funded museums should be “none” or “not much.” Just 17 percent of Republicans seemed to take the president’s position: that he should have a “great deal” of influence. Coming after a history museum may not be the base-galvanizing issue the White House hopes it is. Industry data support these findings. In a survey this year, Wilkening Consulting, in partnership with the American Alliance of Museums, found that when people were asked whether museums, faced with pressure, should remove content on topics such as slavery and climate change, the majority of conservatives (63 percent) and liberals (83 percent) disagreed. An oft-cited statistic from the same pair of organizations places museums among the most trusted sources of information in American life, falling just behind public libraries and family and friends. It suggests that museums occupy a rare and cozy place in the collective imagination. At a time of high mistrust in not just institutions but also observable reality, people seem to still find a sense of stability in these keepers of public memory. Perhaps it makes sense that Americans would put their last bits of trust in the very places that show them what is physically, tangibly real. For more than a year, the White House has threatened and criticized the Smithsonian, accusing it of spreading divisive narratives and failing to adequately celebrate American history. In recent weeks, the administration has zeroed in on the National Museum of American History, publishing a lengthy report last month decrying exhibits, calling out staff members, and asserting that the museum has fallen victim to “ideological capture” at the hands of a “radical, activist cohort.” During a pair of congressional hearings , the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, attested to her love of this country some half a dozen times while maintaining that telling the American story in all of its complexity is a form of respect for its people. Two days later, Trump announced an executive order that would effectively plaster untrustworthy on signs outside the National Museum of American History, like an explicit content label on a CD. The administration ordered the National Park Service to put up the signage in front of the museum to correct what it claims is “inaccurate information” and to share the findings of its report, which claims that the current leadership of the Smithsonian and the history museum cannot be trusted to tell the American story. [ Read: How the Smithsonian could fall ] Right-wing media organizations have echoed this messaging, and since the hearings, Fox News has published dozens of clips and articles criticizing the Smithsonian and scrutinizing its leadership’s pay, highlighting months-old proposed budget cuts, and tallying the number of “liberal items” in a recent exhibit. The Smithsonian, which is partially government-funded , has faced partisan flare-ups over the years. A controversy over how to display the airplane that dropped the atomic bomb over Hiroshima compelled a museum director to resign in 1995. In 2010, Smithsonian leadership removed from the walls of the National Portrait Gallery an artwork showing a crucifix with ants crawling on it after a right-wing outcry. But these incidents involved single exhibits. Now the White House is making a much more comprehensive case against an entire museum and the institution to which it belongs. With the ordered signs, which will direct visitors to Trump-preferred sources of information, the White House is stepping between visitors and historic objects as though to say: Don’t trust what you see inside. Choose us instead. This is where museums and friends and family actually share something in common. Culture wars thrive on the unknown. But museums are an in-person activity. “It’s you directly with that artwork or you directly with that specimen, whatever it is. That object feels like it’s speaking directly to you as a trustworthy thing from the past. That in and of itself lends a lot of credibility,” Susie Wilkening, who runs the American Alliance of Museums’ research about museums and trust, told me. Max van Balgooy, a professor of museum studies at the George Washington University, had similar thoughts: “If you see the gun that John Wilkes Booth used or the chair sat in by John Hancock, you’re sort of faced with the truth,” he told me. “You can’t argue with the real stuff.” Museums weren’t always the hubs of knowledge they are today. They had to both differentiate themselves from the likes of P. T. Barnum’s “museum” as serious scholarly enterprises, devoid of exaggeration and fakes, and invite in ordinary visitors. At the National Museum of History and Technology, which opened in 1964 and went on to become the National Museum of American History, curators strived not just to show objects but also to tell stories, enhanced with well-designed spaces. In the early days, these stories largely celebrated technological progress: When Daniel Boorstin started as the history museum’s director, in 1969, he nodded to the political ruptures of the era and said, “Here, we emphasize the positive. Without denying our failures, we underline and dramatize our successes.” But as more academics joined the museum, they began to stress questions of who, exactly, benefited from American progress, and worked other critical themes into exhibits. The trend—moving from the rah-rah to the sober—was exemplified by a 1987 exhibition that commemorated the bicentennial of the American Constitution and detailed the abuses of Japanese American internment camps. Unlike with other kinds of institutions, such as news sites, naysayers can’t easily form museum alternatives aligned with their perspective. (Partisan museums often struggle to compete with mainstream institutions in terms of historical artifacts.) Part of a museum’s trustworthiness may simply come down to the basic fact that it owns these objects and shows them in an authoritative-looking building. Darryl Hart, a history professor at Hillsdale College, an institution that has worked with the Trump administration on education topics, suggested that museumgoers typically don’t think to critique what they see. “For some people, it’s simply part of what they do on a vacation, and I think they check a box,” he told me. “My sense is, people really are going there fairly innocently, not looking for an agenda.” [ Read: First the Kennedy Center, now the Smithsonian ] The data concur. “On the whole, museums are not believed by the American public to have a political agenda,” Colleen Dilenschneider, the founder of Impacts Experience, a market-research firm that examines perceptions of cultural institutions, told me. Her research, which relies on data from the National Awareness, Attitudes, and Usage Study, found that as of July 1, fewer than a quarter of Americans surveyed believed that museums had political agendas—compared with well over half who believed the same of news sources. Liberals and conservatives both overwhelmingly agreed with the statement that museums are “welcoming to people like me.” Dilenschneider said that “the most shared characteristic of any person in the United States who’s visited a museum in the last year is that they self-identify as a white, non-Hispanic individual” and added that “there are people who are used to hearing their story and they trust that they will continue to hear their story.” Where the story comes from, though, is less clear. Museums contain an essential paradox: They feel transparent because you can walk in and see the work they do. At the same time, the hand behind that work is less visible: As van Balgooy put it, creditless wall texts can read like “the voice of God.” This impersonal feeling is nearly a definitional feature of institutional trust, Oliver Schilke, the director of the Center for Trust Studies at the University of Arizona, told me. “It’s more a trust in a category of things rather than in specific individuals or counterparts,” he said. This slight distance allows us to form an idealized view on an institution. Putting the spotlight on real people behind it can degrade that trust if they’re being attacked or discredited, as happened during the often-acrimonious Smithsonian hearings last month. At times, lawmakers seemed to be speaking directly to their supporters online, such as when Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina demanded that the history museum’s director tell her whether she believes that men can become women. When Victoria Cain, a professor at Northeastern University who studies the history of museums and education, described museums’ role in life today, she made them sound like a tonic to the most charged parts of contemporary discourse. Akin to secular churches, museums have taken on a ritualistic quality, she told me: “You can go be in a common space with other people in an act of appreciation.” In this regard, museums aren’t just a last bastion of public faith—they’re a rare, shared, bipartisan cultural space. These days, many people lament the ways that we have retreated into information silos, full of others who agree with us. But you can’t chop up Thomas Jefferson’s desk and give half of it to the right and half to the left. If we all want to see the desk where the Declaration of Independence was written, we’re going to have to learn, first, to be in the same room.

items.title: Maférinya : deux morts et deux blessés graves dans une collision entre deux motos
items.description: Un grave accident de la circulation s'est produit dans la matinée de ce mardi 4 août 2026, aux environs de 6 heures, à Yoroya, dans le district de Fanyé, relevant de la sous-préfecture de Maferinyah. Selon les informations recueillies sur place, deux motocyclettes sont violemment entrées en collision. La première, en provenance de Fandié, transportait trois personnes, tandis que la seconde, qui venait de Maferinyah, avait deux occupants à son bord. Le bilan provisoire fait état de deux morts sur le coup et de deux blessés graves. Les deux victimes décédées se trouvaient sur la moto en provenance de Maférinyah. D'après les premiers éléments de l'enquête, le conducteur de cette motocyclette aurait tenté de dépasser un véhicule avant de se retrouver face à la moto arrivant en sens inverse. La collision, d'une extrême violence, n'a laissé aucune chance aux deux occupants, qui ont succombé sur les lieux. Les corps des victimes ainsi que les blessés ont été évacués vers le Centre de santé amélioré de Maferinyah, où les survivants sont actuellement pris en charge. Les personnes décédées ont été identifiées comme étant Lamine Soumah , surnommé « Barrage Callé », et M'Mah Ténin Guilavogui , originaire de Foulawa et employée de l'usine Fatala de Yoroyah. Une enquête a été ouverte afin de déterminer les circonstances exactes de ce drame et d'établir les responsabilités.

Garango : Le commissariat de police du secteur 3 inauguré pour renforcer la proximité avec les populations
items.description: À Garango, la sécurité change d'adresse. Un ancien site jadis occupé par les pandores ouvre une nouvelle page de son histoire en devenant le commissariat de police du secteur 3. Bien plus qu'une simple inauguration, cet événement a marqué, ce 1ᵉʳ août 2026, un rapprochement concret entre la Police nationale et les populations, tout en renforçant le dispositif sécuritaire d'une ville en pleine expansion. La cérémonie d'ouverture a réuni le directeur général de la Police nationale, l'inspecteur général de police Thierry Dofizouho Tuina, des autorités administratives, coutumières et régionales, ainsi qu'une foule nombreuse. Le secrétaire général de la région du Nakambé, Tasséré Nacoulma, a procédé à la coupure symbolique du ruban, donnant ainsi le top départ des activités de cette nouvelle unité. La sécurité de proximité au cœur de la stratégie Désormais doté de deux commissariats, Garango améliore son maillage sécuritaire afin de rapprocher davantage les services de police des citoyens et de garantir des interventions plus rapides. Cette réalisation s'inscrit dans la mise en œuvre de la vision « Innovation stratégique et opérationnelle pour une sécurité au quotidien (ISOQ) », qui fait de la proximité avec les populations un levier majeur de l'action policière. Face aux agents affectés dans cette nouvelle structure, le directeur général de la Police nationale a insisté sur la qualité de l'accueil réservé aux usagers. Il les a invités à faire preuve d'intégrité, de discipline, de probité et d'exemplarité, tout en incarnant les valeurs de policiers révolutionnaires, progressistes et vertueux au service exclusif des citoyens. Le patron de la Police a également lancé un appel aux populations afin qu'elles s'approprient ce nouveau commissariat, fréquentent ses services et renforcent leur collaboration avec les forces de sécurité. Selon lui, la lutte contre l'insécurité repose autant sur l'engagement des forces de l'ordre que sur la participation active des communautés. Développement local et services aux citoyens Le représentant du gouverneur de la région du Nakambé, Tasséré Nacoulma, tout comme le président de la délégation spéciale de Garango, Timothée N. Zombré, ont salué cette infrastructure qu'ils considèrent comme un investissement majeur pour la paix, la sécurité et le développement de la commune. En marge de l'inauguration, l'Office national d'identification (ONI) a rapproché ses services des populations en organisant une opération spéciale d'établissement de la carte nationale d'identité de l'AES, permettant à de nombreux citoyens d'effectuer leurs démarches sur place. La cérémonie s'est achevée par la plantation d'un manguier, symbole d'enracinement et d'avenir. Avant de quitter Garango, le directeur général de la Police nationale a effectué une visite au premier commissariat de la ville, où il a salué une initiative citoyenne visant à améliorer le cadre de travail des policiers. Avec l'ouverture du commissariat du secteur 3, la Police nationale franchit une nouvelle étape dans son ambition de bâtir une sécurité de proximité, fondée sur la confiance, la collaboration et une présence renforcée au cœur des communautés. items.title: Yacine Titraoui, le « Verratti algérien », débarque au RC Lens pour la Ligue des champions
items.description: Le milieu international algérien Yacine Titraoui change de club et disputera la Ligue des champions la saison prochaine. Formé au Paradou AC à l’image de Ramy Bensebaini et Youcef Atal, celui qui est surnommé le « Verratti algérien », pour ses qualités qui ressemblent à celles de l’ancien milieu international italien, vient de quitter le club belge de Charleroi pour poser ses valises au RC Lens en Ligue 1 française. Il remplace numériquement Mamadou Sangaré parti à Brentford en Angleterre. Après deux saisons passées à Charleroi où il a montré ses qualités, Titraoui a signé un contrat jusqu’en 2031 avec les Sang et Or. Le RC Lens accueille Yacine Titroui, un joueur avec un « bagage technique haut de gamme » À 23 ans, le milieu axial algérien a un « bagage technique haut de gamme et figurait parmi les meilleurs milieux du championnat belge ces deux dernières saisons », dit de lui Jean-Louis Leca, directeur sportif du Racing Club de Lens qui a terminé la saison à la 2 e place du championnat de France, derrière l’indétrônable PSG. Un dernier message du petit prince algérien. Prenez soin de lui @RCLens #RCSC #NapoleonScore pic.twitter.com/liFKXv1Urc — Royal Charleroi Sporting Club (@SportCharleroi) August 3, 2026 Leca ajoute que Titraoui va apporter au RC Lens sa « faculté à jouer sous pression et constamment vers l’avant ». « Humainement, c’est un garçon simple et travailleur qui nous rejoint », ajoute-il sur le site du club lensois. Pour lui, l’international algérien « incarne l’avenir de l’équipe d’Algérie et celui du Racing ». Un métronome au cœur du jeu Inlassable coureur et chef d'orchestre de l’entrejeu, Yacine Titraoui rejoint le Racing après deux saisons abouties au @SportCharleroi . Récent participant à la @FIFAWorldCup avec l'Algérie , le milieu s'engage jusqu’en 2031. #LesLensois2 — Racing Club de Lens (@RCLens) August 3, 2026 Le RC Lens ne tarit pas d’éloges sur son nouveau milieu axial qu’il présente comme un « inépuisable travailleur ». « ll est aussi le joueur de Jupiler Pro League (championnat de Belgique) qui effectue le plus de courses progressives et de distance en sprint ». En équipe d’Algérie, Yacine Titraoui a été retenu par Vladimir Petkovic pour la Coupe du monde 2026, mais il ne l’a pas fait jouer, lui préférant Nabil Bentaleb, Ramiz Zerrouki ou Hicham Boudaoui. Avec le départ du technicien suisse, le nouveau milieu de terrain du RC Lens devrait avoir sa chance avec les Fennecs. Le futur sélectionneur devrait poursuivre le projet de reconstruction de l’équipe nationale dans lequel Titraoui pourrait avoir sa place. items.title: Congé présidentiel : l’armée réaffirme sa loyauté au président Doumbouya et appelle les Guinéens au calme
items.description: À la suite du communiqué annonçant le départ en congé annuel du président de la République, le chef d'état-major général des armées, le général Ibrahima Sory Bangoura, a lu sur les antennes de la télévision nationale un communiqué pour rassurer les Guinéens sur la continuité de l'État et la stabilité du pays. S'exprimant au nom de l'ensemble des forces de défense et de sécurité, le chef d'état-major a affirmé la « fidélité constante » et la « loyauté indéfectible » des forces armées envers le président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, ainsi qu'envers les institutions de la République et le peuple de Guinée. Dans ce communiqué, les forces de défense et de sécurité réitèrent leur engagement à poursuivre le processus de mise en place des institutions de la République, conformément aux dispositions de la Constitution. Elles réaffirment également leur détermination à accompagner les actions de refondation de l'État, estimant que leurs effets sont déjà perceptibles par les populations. Le Général Ibrahima Sory Bangoura assure par ailleurs que les forces de défense et de sécurité demeureront pleinement mobilisées pour garantir la stabilité intérieure et préserver l'intégrité du territoire national, deux conditions qu'il considère comme essentielles à la poursuite de la dynamique de développement engagée dans le pays. « En conséquence, les forces de défense et de sécurité useront de tous les moyens indispensables à l'accomplissement de leurs missions régaliennes », souligne le communiqué. Face aux rumeurs et aux informations circulant sur les réseaux sociaux à l'occasion du congé du chef de l'État, l'état-major général des armées invite les citoyens à ne pas céder à la désinformation et à poursuivre sereinement leurs activités quotidiennes. Le communiqué s'achève par un message de courtoisie adressé au président de la République. Les forces de défense et de sécurité lui souhaitent, ainsi qu'à sa famille, d'agréables congés annuels. Cette sortie du chef d'état-major intervient quelques heures après l'annonce officielle du départ en congé annuel du président Mamadi Doumbouya, dans un contexte marqué par de nombreuses spéculations sur les réseaux sociaux. Par cette déclaration, le haut commandement militaire entend rassurer l'opinion publique sur la continuité des institutions et le maintien de la stabilité du pays.

items.title: The Danger of Trump’s Anti-Communist Rhetoric
items.description: Sign up for our newsletter about national security here . K arl Marx wrote that political actors often borrow the language and symbols of earlier struggles to wage their own battles. So perhaps he would have been unsurprised to hear the Trump administration resurrect the political rhetoric of the Cold War fight against Marxism. President Trump, at Wheeler High School in the Atlanta suburbs earlier this summer, mentioned communism or communist 15 times, starting less than a minute into his hour-plus speech: “Communism is the single greatest threat to our country and its history—including even World War I and World War II, Pearl Harbor, 9/11,” he claimed. “I think it’s the greatest threat that I’ve ever seen to our country.” Last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio convened political leaders, counterterrorism professionals, and law-enforcement officers from 66 countries for what the State Department billed as an extraordinary gathering aimed at confronting “a transnational threat.” From a podium flanked by world flags, Rubio spoke of the need to combat the far left around the world. “This is a distinctive and unique evil,” he said. “They can call themselves anti-capitalist or anti-imperialist or communist or anarchist or Marxist, but the fundamental character is always the same.” The State Department even has a culprit in mind, last week releasing a 100-page report that characterized Cuba as “posing a unique threat” to American security. Never mind that the island nation of 11 million people lost its chief sponsor with the Soviet Union’s collapse and is so economically strapped that the regime rations electricity and gas. The official line of the U.S. government is that Havana has backed “left-wing terrorism” inside the United States—including “violent BLM militants” and “Antifa terror cells”—and provides a refuge for communism in the Western Hemisphere. “The Cuba that they’re describing, going back to the ’60s and onward, doesn’t exist anymore,” Ted Piccone, a senior foreign-policy adviser for the Clinton administration, told us. “I think they’re just fighting an old ghost in old battles.” From the standpoint of the White House, however, reviving communism as a boogeyman is a way to tie together two very current objectives. On the home front, experts told us that the vilification of Communists could be an attempt to shift the focus away from painful pocketbook issues such as higher gas prices and inflation, and to paint Democrats, and democratic socialists in particular, as anti-American ahead of the midterms. Overseas, fighting Marxism, especially in Latin America, injects principle into the administration’s desire for dominance in the Western Hemisphere, which so far has led to the removal of a leftist dictator in Venezuela and laid the groundwork for the overthrow of the regime in Havana. Tommy Pigott, a State Department spokesperson, said in a statement that the United States will “not ignore the threat posed by a regime 90 miles off our coast intent on undermining the national security of the American people through espionage and the spread of its failed, insidious ideology.” Others see less ideological combat, more exercise of American muscle. “The idea is to get rid of any government in the Western Hemisphere that’s not willing to toe the line,” William LeoGrande, a former dean of American University’s School of Public Affairs, told us. “It started with Venezuela, obviously, and now turned to Cuba.” He added, “If I was Daniel Ortega,” Nicaragua’s autocratic ruler, “I might be a little worried that I’d be next.” [ Read: How to break Cuba ] U.S. voters may regard the revival of the “Reds under the bed” scare as a desperate attempt by an unpopular president to bolster his party’s election chances. Others may see Rubio using an outdated threat as cover to achieve greater American influence. But the push is already having an effect elsewhere, as other Latin American governments paint pro-democracy protesters as Marxists intent on undermining public order to justify crackdowns. T rump and his allies have repeatedly described Democrats as socialists or Communists, regardless of how moderate those Democrats’ positions were. During the 2016 presidential campaign, he referred to Senator Bernie Sanders, a democratic socialist, as just a “socialist.” And the October before the 2018 midterms, Trump wrote in an op-ed in USA Today that the “new Democrats are radical socialists” who want to introduce “open-borders socialism,” and he warned that their economic policies were modeled after the socialist policies of Nicolás Maduro’s Venezuela. He never used the word communism , though, and despite his warnings, Democrats took control of the House. By 2024, Trump was calling his rival for the presidency “Comrade Kamala.” This June, the president again started describing Democratic candidates as “Communist.” Speaking at the Faith & Freedom Coalition’s policy conference, Trump declared : “It’s becoming a communist party. These are not social Democrats; these are hard-core, godless Communists.” A Reuters analysis revealed that Trump invoked the word communism more than 80 times in the two weeks leading up to July 8. The shift followed primary victories by democratic-socialist candidates in New York, California, and Colorado, as well as last year’s sweeping victory by the DSA standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani to become mayor of New York City. Polls currently suggest that the Democrats could win one or both chambers of Congress in November. “The Democrats’ full-blown embrace of socialism and communism is a mortal threat to American liberty,” the White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told us in a statement. “President Trump will never allow America to become a socialist or communist country.” Others in the administration, including Vice President Vance, have echoed Trump’s rhetoric. But no member has been more fervent in his public disdain for Communists than Rubio. His anti-communism is deeply personal. The secretary, the first of Latino descent to serve in the role, is the grandson of Cuban exiles who fled the island as Fidel Castro took power, settling in South Florida, where Rubio grew up. “Marco’s talked about this a lot—growing up in a Cuban American community, you hear the stories: firsthand accounts about repression; about not having basic freedoms; about watching an economy just collapse under that system,” Cesar Conda, Rubio’s former Senate chief of staff, told us. “That stuff shapes you. I think it shaped him, from a really young age.” That hatred of communism became a constant reprise through Rubio’s career in local and state politics in Florida, in the U.S. Senate, and in the Trump administration. “It’s not complicated once you understand where he comes from,” Conda said. “It’s personal, it’s family, it’s ideology, and yeah, there’s a strategic piece to it, too. But the family history—that’s the big one. That’s really where it starts.” Rubio does not hold all Communists to the same standard. Conda recalled that Rubio, while a Senator in 2014, “said he’d never wanted to set foot in Communist China” because of his contempt for communist regimes. His criticism of China’s human-rights record put Rubio on a Chinese sanctions list in 2020—twice. (Rubio’s trip to Beijing with Trump this year was his first.) But Rubio told reporters late last month that China, still home to the world’s largest and most successful Communist Party, would remain a diplomatic partner to the United States. “These are the two most powerful economies in the world, two large militaries, two nuclear powers,” Rubio said. “We have to have a relationship with China, and we want it to be as positive as it possibly can be.” (Imagine President Ronald Reagan saying the same about the Soviets.) Rubio has paid relatively little attention to the other nominally left-wing regime in North Korea. Instead, the administration has depicted Western Europe as a new hotbed of Marxism. The State Department, in recent months, placed four European left-wing groups, including the Germany-based Antifa Ost, on blacklists designed to isolate terrorists, choke off their funding, and protect national security. Advocates of this approach point to an uptick in left-wing political violence. The Trump administration has claimed that left-wing extremists and anarchists are responsible for most terror attacks in Europe, pointing to data from 2022. American officials also emphasize the more than 40 percent increase in violence attributed to left-wing extremism in Germany. Other data tell a different story. In 2025, the European Union member states recorded 11 completed attacks by left-wing extremist groups. But only about a third of completed terror attacks in the EU have been attributed to left-wing actors over the past three years, according to Europol, the EU’s law-enforcement agency. (The highest number of completed attacks was attributed to ethno-nationalist and separatist groups—primarily in France—while jihadist groups were responsible for the largest number of foiled or failed attacks.) In Germany, right-wing extremists continue to account for the largest share of political violence. The German far-right party AfD, which the government deemed an extremist group last year, leads nationwide popularity polls. Farther east, several states that were once Soviet satellites have swung right. Many European countries that used to be under communist control now appear to be on Trump’s side. [ Read: Europe’s far right is turning on Trump ] I n the Trump administration’s ideal world , Cuba might go the way of Venezuela, where military intervention and Maduro’s seizure forced the country into close partnership with the United States. The administration has been piling pressure on Havana to expand its private sector (which would allow greater access for U.S. companies) and to make changes at the top, with the threat of military action if the regime doesn’t yield. The prolonged war with Iran has complicated that campaign, and produced skepticism even among the president’s supporters of the wisdom of foreign intervention. “Some sort of military adventure in Cuba on the heels of a very unpopular war in Iran would be political suicide,” Christopher Hernandez-Roy, the acting director of the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told us. “So they have to point to some other things, such as painting Cuba as a geopolitical adversary that’s spreading communism around the world, which is kind of silly.” But it’s a strategy that other leaders have used successfully. Argentinian President Javier Milei, a Trump ally, has described much of his domestic opposition not as fellow citizens with competing ideas but as agents of an ideological enemy. Labor organizers, feminist movements, and left-leaning political groups have all been labeled “Communists” or willing accomplices to a communist project. What the targets believe is almost irrelevant. Once political opponents are cast as part of a larger ideological conspiracy, Milei and his allies can treat them as a threat to democratic life. Milei introduced, then expanded, a sweeping campaign to limit labor strikes, street demonstrations, and other forms of organized dissent. Federal security forces last year moved aggressively to clear picket lines, disperse demonstrations, and prevent protesters from blocking roads after the passage of economic reforms. Protest organizers now face the prospect of criminal investigations, financial penalties, and state surveillance. Trump’s labeling of his political opponents as “Communists” may be a transparent ploy. And Rubio’s portrayal of Havana as a principal exporter of left-wing terror may be impossible to reconcile with the reality of modern-day Cuba. But the administration’s anti-communist vocabulary has nonetheless been embraced by governments far beyond Washington. The result isn’t a new Cold War. It’s the spread of an old political lexicon that can be used to cast political opponents as representatives of a specter that most people thought had long been dispatched.

items.title: Le nettoyeur public de Balacoss (Saint-Louis)
items.description: Au quartier Balacoss de Saint-Louis, un homme a choisi de transformer son indignation en action. Chaque matin, bien avant le lever du soleil, il balaie, nettoie, arrose les arbres et veille sur sa rue avec le soin que l'on accorde à son propre foyer. Ce citoyen exemplaire, c'est Malick Ndaw, affectueusement appelé « El Hadji ». À près de 60 ans, ce Saint-Louisien au teint noir, à la silhouette fine et discrète, est devenu le symbole d'un dévouement civique qui force le respect. SAINT-LOUIS – Au premier regard, rien ne laisse deviner que cette rue se trouve dans une ville régulièrement confrontée aux problèmes d'insalubrité. Le pavage est impeccable, les trottoirs propres. Les arbres, parfaitement entretenus, offrent une ombre rafraîchissante. En plus, aucun déchet ne vient ternir ce décor. Au quartier Balacoss, à Saint-Louis, cette rue est devenue une référence. Derrière cette transformation se cache un seul homme : Malick Ndaw, dit El Hadji. Originaire de Saint-Louis, il a longtemps vécu à Dakar avant de revenir dans sa ville natale, il y a moins d'une dizaine d'années. Le constat qu'il fait à son retour le choque : la ville qu'il avait connue propre et accueillante semble avoir perdu une partie de son éclat. Lorsque sa rue est réhabilitée avec des pavés, il décide d'apporter sa propre pierre à l'édifice. « Je me suis dit qu'il fallait aussi que je participe. Depuis cinq à six ans, c'est devenu mon quotidien », a confié M. Ndaw. Chaque jour, son réveil sonne vers quatre heures du matin. Après son café, il sort, balai à la main. Il nettoie la chaussée, vide les poubelles, arrose les arbres et entretient les espaces verts. À sept heures, lorsque les premiers habitants quittent leurs maisons, la rue est déjà impeccable. Tout le matériel est financé avec ses propres moyens, même si quelques voisins lui apportent, de temps à autre, une aide ponctuelle. Son initiative ne tarde pas à attirer les regards. Sur les réseaux sociaux, comme auprès des autorités locales, cette rue est souvent citée en exemple. Plusieurs habitants d'autres secteurs de Balacoss et même d'autres quartiers de Saint-Louis se sont inspirés de son modèle pour organiser, à leur tour, des opérations de nettoyage. Mais, pour El Hadji, l'essentiel n'est pas la reconnaissance. Son combat est avant tout celui du changement des mentalités. Pas besoin de décorations « Notre environnement nous appartient. Il n'appartient pas aux autres de venir faire le travail à notre place », a-t-il insisté. Il regrette toutefois que les comportements peinent encore à évoluer durablement. Selon lui, les campagnes ponctuelles de salubrité ne suffisent pas. La propreté doit devenir un réflexe quotidien. Son engagement lui a valu plusieurs distinctions citoyennes et même une promesse de décoration, lors d'une rencontre avec l'ancien président Macky Sall, restée sans suite. Une situation qu'il évoque sans amertume. « Je n'attends pas de récompense. Ce que je fais, c'est un engagement citoyen », a-t-il simplement affirmé. À travers son action, Malick Ndaw rappelle qu'une ville ne devient pas propre uniquement grâce aux services publics. Elle le devient surtout « lorsque des citoyens décident de montrer l'exemple ». Dans une époque où l'on attend souvent tout des pouvoirs publics, cet habitant de Balacoss prouve qu'un simple balai, beaucoup de volonté et une constance sans faille peuvent transformer tout un cadre de vie. Son rêve est désormais de voir chaque rue de Saint-Louis adopter la même culture du civisme, car, dit-il, « quand on s'organise, on réussit de belles choses ». Jeanne SAGNA (Correspondante)

items.title: Un verano contra el fuego en una base de León helitransportada inútil: “Tardamos hora y media en llegar en coche y volando serían 15 minutos”
items.description: La base helitransportada de El Oterico (León) costó casi dos millones de euros, se anunció en 2022 y se destacó que a finales de 2023 estaría “prácticamente terminada”. Los bomberos que trabajan en ella en el verano de 2026 no la han podido utilizar hasta hace unos días para los medios aéreos para los que se concibió porque incumplía lo necesario en términos de seguridad y operatividad y no terminaba de estar concluida : “Tenerla inoperativa un 1 de agosto sería un error terrible”. La base, con suelo de arenisca que inhabilita la mayor parte de sus pistas, está cerrada simplemente contra el ganado por un pastor eléctrico que han dispuesto los brigadistas y los depósitos de combustible han pasado semanas desprecintados. Pese a la reciente apertura, apenas hay cobertura ni cuentan con teléfono fijo y tampoco funcionan las duchas en unas instalaciones clave para dominar la montaña central leonesa, recurrentemente castigada por los fuegos como los que a menudo se ven muy cerca desde Oterico. Un bombero expresa así el trastorno de incendios recientes: “Tardamos hora y media en coche y volando serían 15 minutos”. Seguir leyendo
